thesis: REITs are the one asset class hurt by both arms of this regime, which is why the position stays on while the TLT short comes off: a 5.00% 10-year reprices cap rates against existing portfolios, and a Fed that hiked in September and has 73% December hike odds priced keeps refinancing costs climbing into 2027. IYR has lagged SPY by 13.96% over three months and has now bounced 5.0% off its 140-day low back under its falling 50-day at 99.19 — a laggard retesting resistance into a known 14:00 ET binary.
key_risk: The target at 90.50 sits below the 140-day low of 93.29, so the trade requires a break to new lows rather than a retest. A dovish surprise at 14:00 ET, or the weak 29k September payroll print turning the Fed back toward easing, would re-rate the whole long-duration complex at once and the stop is only 1.93 ATR away.
counter_argument: September nonfarm payrolls rose just 29,000 and the 10-year has already fallen from 5.17% in late September to 5.00%, so the bond market is beginning to price a policy error rather than more inflation. That rally is exactly what is taking the TLT short off the book. It does not rescue REITs, though: a recession bid lowers the discount rate and the cash flow at the same time, and occupancy and rent growth are what gets repriced second.

catalyst.event: FOMC statement and Warsh press conference - the print this short was being carried into
catalyst.action: EXIT. Hold into 14:00 ET with the 82.00 stop UNCHANGED, as the 2026-10-25 plan said, then be flat by Friday close whatever the statement says. Do NOT widen the stop and do NOT add. No new entry at any price.

thesis: This is a close instruction, not a re-pitch. The short was opened at 79.90 on the view that term premium drives the long end higher; TLT is at 81.63, which is 0.47 ATR from the 82.00 stop and 7.5% from the 75.70 target, so almost the whole remaining distribution is a loss. What actually happened is a flattening, not a steepening: between late September and 10/26 the 10-year fell from 5.17% to 5.00% while December hike odds rose from 42% to 73%, so the front end repriced hawkish and the long end rallied. That is the bond market pricing a policy error on a 29k payroll print, and it is the opposite of the trade.
key_risk: Exiting into the one catalyst left is the risk: a hawkish Warsh presser at 14:30 ET could take TLT straight to the 75.70 target and this instruction gives that up. That is accepted deliberately - 82.00 is where the thesis was defined to be wrong and it is 0.47 ATR away, so the trade is being closed on geometry rather than on a new macro view.
counter_argument: The strongest case for holding is that the macro thesis has strengthened, not weakened: all 100 Reuters-polled economists forecast a December hike and the 10-year is at 5.00% with CPI at 3.7%. True, and it is why the long-duration short stays on the book through IYR instead. But a correct thesis in a position with 0.37 of upside room to its stop is not a tradeable edge, and widening 82.00 to survive today is exactly the stop-walking this report has banned.

thesis: Housing is the weak pole of a two-speed economy and the fundamentals got worse while the stocks went up. September pending home sales hit a record-low index reading of 66, builders are cutting prices at a record pace, and the 30-year fixed averaged 7.32% in the week of 10/22. ITB nevertheless rallied 10.1% off its 400-day low of 82.08, most of it in one 5.4% session on 10/22 that was a rotation out of falling tech into cheap cyclicals rather than any housing news - XHB +3.8% and Lennar +9% on the day the record-low pending sales print landed. The ETF now sits at 90.35, under a 200-day SMA at 96.32, with the largest builder reporting tomorrow before the open.
key_risk: The stop of record is the problem, and it is being left alone on purpose: 3.80 from entry is 1.57 ATR against a 1.8 ATR ETF floor, so an ordinary two-day bounce stops this out on noise. It cannot be fixed either - widening it to the real level overhead, the 200-day at 96.32, puts risk at 6.52 against 8.30 of reward and collapses the ratio to 1.27. So this position is a hold-only; the right size for it is the size already on.
counter_argument: The bull case is that builders are a rate-cut call option and the 29k payroll print brings cuts forward, which is roughly what 10/22 traded on. Two things answer it: the Fed hiked in September and 100 of 100 polled economists expect another hike in December, so the near-term rate path is the wrong way; and record-pace price cuts are gross margin compression that shows up in reported numbers regardless of where rates go next, which is exactly what tomorrow prints.

catalyst.action: TAKE PROFIT and be flat. Sell half at today open, work the balance to 70.50, and be flat by the 2026-10-29 close - ahead of Friday BMO, not into it. Stop of record stays 60.80. Do NOT flip short.

thesis: This is an exit, and the reason is better than the one given on 10/27. The +9.0% in this position is a war premium that has already been paid: there is an active US-Iran war with exchanged strikes, Brent is ~112-116 and WTI ~100-103 against ~90 two months ago, and roughly 9.5 mbd left Hormuz last week, about 30% below pre-war normal. Continued war is now in the price - XLE sits 2.36% off its 140-day high and 29.63% above its low. What is not in the price is a ceasefire, and Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani officials have travelled to Tehran to discuss ending hostilities. Yesterday the complex traded that: XOM -2.51%, CVX -1.63%, XLE -2.05%.
key_risk: Exiting a physical shortage because diplomats are travelling is the risk, and it is why the instruction is to sell into strength over two sessions rather than dump at the open. If talks collapse or the US strikes again, Hormuz at -30% of normal flow gaps crude higher and this gives up the best part of the move.
counter_argument: The bull case is simple and strong: the disruption is physical, 30% of Hormuz flow is a genuine shortage, inventories do not rebuild on a communique, and XOM and CVX report into the highest realisations in two years on Friday. Granted - but that is an argument for the position having worked, which it has at +9.0%. It is not an argument for holding a geopolitical premium through a 2-day, 5-name earnings cluster while the counterparty is in ceasefire talks. The asymmetry, not the direction, is what changed.

thesis: Financials are the one sector this rate regime pays rather than punishes, which is why it is the long that stays while the duration shorts get trimmed. A front end at 3.88% with roughly 80% odds priced on a December hike widens asset yields faster than deposit costs, and a 10y-2y curve at +0.29 that is steepening from the long end restores the carry banks lost for two years. XLF is at 55.88 against a 54.23 entry, +10.83% off its 140-day low, sitting on a 50-day SMA at 56.00 it has been grinding against, with the target at 57.60 inside the 58.60 range high rather than beyond it.
key_risk: Banks are a credit call, not just a rate call, and a Fed hiking into +29k payrolls is how credit cracks. The specific thing to watch is consumer and CRE provisions: the same 5.00% 10-year that widens net interest margin is what is repricing the commercial real estate book, and this report is short IYR precisely because that repricing is happening. If the 14:30 ET presser lands as a policy error rather than a hawkish hold, XLF is a cyclical and trades like one.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that the curve is flattening, not steepening - the 10-year fell from 5.17% in late September to 5.00% while December hike odds went 42% to 73%, which compresses exactly the carry this thesis claims. That is real and it is why the TLT short is being closed today. It does not break the bank case, because a higher front end reprices floating-rate assets immediately while deposit betas lag, so the near-term margin tailwind arrives whether or not the long end cooperates.

thesis: Small caps are the cohort a hiking Fed actually reaches, because Russell 2000 balance sheets carry floating-rate debt that reprices with the front end rather than with a refinancing calendar. The front end is at 3.88% with roughly 80% priced on a December hike, and IWM is lagging SPY on every window measured - minus 0.47% on 1m, minus 8.42% on 3m, minus 5.86% on 6m. The index divergence makes the point: SPY sits 1.53% off its high on its 20- and 50-day, while IWM is 8.19% off its high and below its 50-day at 285.37, having spent all October trapped in a 269.88-284.64 range it is now in the top of.
key_risk: This is the third idea on one driver, alongside IYR and ITB, which is exactly at this report correlation cap - a dovish 14:30 ET presser hits all three on the same afternoon and the book has no fourth leg to absorb it. The specific invalidation is a reclaim of 285.40, where the October high cluster and the 50-day sit on top of each other; two closes above it and the range broke upward rather than down.
counter_argument: The bull case is that small caps are a levered rate-cut call and the September payroll print of +29,000 brings cuts forward - and that is roughly what traded on 10/22, when the rotation out of falling tech lifted the cheap cyclical complex. Two answers. The near-term path is the wrong way: the Fed hiked in September, 100 of 100 Reuters-polled economists forecast a December hike, and live Kalshi orderbooks put it at ~80%. And a stalling labour market is not the rescue it looks like for this cohort, because small caps are hit by both arms - the funding cost rises with the front end while the revenue line is the first to feel a +29k economy. A pause that arrives because growth broke is not a small-cap bid.

catalyst.action: CLOSE. Sell the full position at the open. This resolves a contradiction rather than calling a top - the report cannot be long building products and short homebuilders on the same housing data. No re-entry until the invalidation below reverses.

thesis: This is a close instruction. The position was opened at 76.50 on a housing-recovery accumulation thesis and is at 76.02, essentially flat after 70 days, which makes the exit nearly free. The reason to take it is that the same research that justifies holding the ITB short kills this: September pending home sales printed a record-low index reading of 66, builders are cutting prices at a record pace, and the 30-year fixed averaged 7.32% in the week of 10/22 against a Fed that hiked in September with ~80% priced on another hike in December. Boise Cascade sells wood products into single-family starts. Holding it alongside a homebuilder short is paying two spreads to be flat on one view.
key_risk: Closing a long_term accumulation at the flat point is how you sell the bottom, and that is the live risk - BCC is 14.03% off its high and +16.95% off its low, so this is not an exit from strength. Accepted anyway, because the thesis has a stated invalidation and the invalidation has now happened: pending sales at a record low with builders discounting is the volume and pricing environment the accumulation case said would improve.
counter_argument: The strongest case for holding is that building products lead housing out of a trough and you must own them before the data turns, which by construction means owning them while the data is bad - and a long_term holding is meant to survive exactly this. Fair, and it is why the position was opened. But the thesis needed the trough to be forming, and record-low pending sales with record-pace price cuts is a trough still deepening. Note also the liquidity: average dollar volume is $25.5m a day, the thinnest instrument in this book, so the time to leave is while the exit is cheap.
